name: let the ending be how many times you chose one way
one_line: Five either-or questions and six endings, where the ending is the count of one kind of answer instead of the path that was taken.
how: Write five questions with two answers each, A or B, and six endings numbered by how many A's. Print the five, a row of five blanks, and a table sending 0 A to one paragraph, 1 A to the next, up to 5. That is eleven pieces of writing. The full tree of the same five choices is thirty-two endings and sixty-three paragraphs, of which one reading sees six: ninety per cent of what gets written is never read. Then the check that makes the form: change any one answer and the ending changes, every time, whichever one it is. Ask for two or three to be tried. Last line, and it cannot be marked: was there one you answered thinking about which ending you wanted rather than about what you would do.

knobs.effect: The tree gives thirty-two endings for sixty-three paragraphs. The sum gives six for eleven. In both, changing any one choice changes the ending; only one of the two fits on a sheet of paper.
Five gives six endings and eleven paragraphs. Three gives four and seven, and a single reversal is too visible. Seven gives eight and fifteen, and the questions begin to outrun the page.

Endings that are simply different can all be arrived at. One ending marked as the successful one turns the sheet into a puzzle with a right set of answers, and the questions stop being about the person.

knobs.knob: whether the paragraphs share the sheet
knobs.effect: All six printed together can all be read, and nothing is lost by choosing. Hiding them takes a fold or an envelope, which is one more thing somebody folds by hand before the afternoon.

where_the_work_is: In the five questions being ones somebody actually has an opinion about. The structure guarantees each one moves the ending; nothing guarantees any of them is worth asking, and that half is written by hand.
breaks: The six paragraphs are on the sheet, so all of them can be read and nothing is really lost by choosing. Nor are these really choices: nothing happens in the world for having made one, and the world here is a sheet that does not change. On 800x480 five questions with two answers each do not fit; five one-line prompts, the blanks and the tally rule do.
